facts.claim: Shawn James & the Shapeshifters' cover of 'The Number of the Beast' is track 6 on the album The Covers, released May 27, 2014 (© and ℗ SHAWN JAMES SOUL INC).
The song was written by Steve Harris and first released by Iron Maiden in 1982. Shawn James and the Shapeshifters' version is a cover.
The Bandcamp credits for The Covers say it was recorded live by Nick Futch. Futch also played drums.
The album's Bandcamp credits list Shawn James on vocals and guitar, Nick Shoulders on harmonica and banjo, Phillip Farris on bass, Chris Overcash on violin, and Baker on mandolin and tenor banjo.
The Covers has 8 tracks. Besides the Iron Maiden song, it includes John the Revelator, God's Gonna Cut You Down, Love Me or Die, American Hearts and A Change Is Gonna Come.
A Bandcamp commenter singled out this track as a favorite. Another commenter said Shawn James doesn't just 'cover' a song, he makes it his own.
In February 2015, Moshville's 'Classic Covers' column featured the band's Maiden cover. It described the band's sound as very laid back rock music.
At an October 2014 show in Wölfersheim, Germany, the band played Iron Maiden's 'The Number of the Beast' and Motörhead's 'Ace of Spades' as covers.
In a 2017 Musikreviews.de interview, Shawn James described himself as a songwriter and author from Chicago, Illinois, and said he is fairly obsessed with mythology, sagas and legends.
Before The Covers, the band released the EPs The Bear and The Wolf in 2013. The Hawk followed in 2014, and the album The Gospel According to Shawn James & the Shapeshifters came in 2015.

research.lineage: A heavy metal classic is reworked in a stripped-down, rootsy blues/folk-rock style by a band whose own work draws on Southern gothic, blues and folk, with hard-rock and metal influences.

draft:
Strip the twin guitars and the galloping bass out of **The Number of the Beast** and what's left is a nightmare told by someone too shaken to shout. Shawn James & the Shapeshifters play Steve Harris's 1982 Iron Maiden song as a slow ballad. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls out arpeggios over a low, sustained bass line. Shawn James sings in a clear, resonant voice, smooth and drawn out, with no harmonies to share the weight. The room is open and lightly reverbed, the texture clean. The Moshville "Classic Covers" column called the band's sound very laid back rock music, and that's the shock of it: the scariest song in the metal canon delivered like a confession at closing time.

The quiet makes you hear what the lyric was always about. Before any torches or chants, the narrator is alone and unsure, trying to "get the memories from my mind" and asking whether what he saw was real. The most frightening image isn't the ritual at all. It's this: "Was a reflection of my warped mind / Staring back at me." The fear points inward. At this tempo the doubt sits in the open, and the horror reads as a person who can't trust their own head.

Then the voice changes hands. Late in the lyric, the speaker stops being the witness and becomes the thing itself: "I'm coming back and I will return." Sung in the same even, sustained way as the frightened verses, that line lands with a creeping calm. The narrator's dread and the beast's promise come out of one mouth in one tone, and the song never says where one ends and the other begins. The chorus repeats "six, six, six" over and over, less a battle cry here than a phrase someone can't stop saying.

The reading fits the record around it. *The Covers* puts this next to "John the Revelator," "God's Gonna Cut You Down," and "A Change Is Gonna Come," songs where judgment and the devil are close, real things. James, a Chicago songwriter, has said he's fairly obsessed with mythology, sagas and legends. That shows here: he treats Harris's B-movie imagery as folklore, something told low by the fire. The album was recorded live by Nick Futch, who also played drums, with Phillip Farris on bass and fiddle, banjo, harmonica and mandolin in the wider lineup. The band brought this one to a stage in Germany in 2014, alongside Motörhead's "Ace of Spades."

Slowed down and sung softly, the song stops being a spectacle about evil and becomes the private terror of seeing your own face in the dark and not being sure it's yours.
